title: Savitri and Satyavan
hook: a king's daughter is so radiant no one dares ask for her, so her father sends her out to choose for herself
carry: make one choice fully your own

segments.voice: Yesterday ended the story of Nala and Damayanti: a trap made of love, a racing chariot, and Kali leaving at last. Your line was tell someone how you'd know them anywhere. Who would know you in any disguise? Day seven hundred ninety-five.

Still in the forest, Yudhishthira has another question, this time for the sage Markandeya. He has watched Draupadi suffer beside him through all of it, the hall, the exile, the forest. Has there ever been a woman as devoted as she is? Markandeya answers the way Brihadashva did. With a story. There was a princess, he says, named Savitri. And her story, like Nala's, starts long before the trouble does, with a father who wanted a child.
screen: `ANOTHER QUESTION IN THE FOREST.` → `MARKANDEYA TELLS A STORY.` → `A PRINCESS NAMED SAVITRI.`

segments.voice: Ashvapati, king of the Madras, is good, generous and childless. So he takes up a discipline: he eats sparingly, keeps his senses in check, and makes offerings with the Savitri mantra, for a long time. At last the goddess Savitri herself rises out of the sacred fire and grants him a daughter. He names the girl after the goddess who gave her. Savitri grows up so radiant that people compare her to a goddess. And here the story takes an unexpected turn. Because she is so splendid, no man dares to ask for her hand. The radiance that should draw suitors keeps them away. Her father is troubled. And he does something unusual. He tells her: go yourself. Find a husband worthy of you, and tell me who he is. So Savitri sets out in a chariot, with her father's old counselors beside her, and travels through forests and hermitages, looking. When she comes home, the sage Narada happens to be sitting with her father. Ashvapati asks her where she has been. And Savitri tells them. There is a king of the Shalvas named Dyumatsena, she says. He lost his sight, and an enemy took his kingdom, and now he lives in a forest hermitage with his wife and his son. That son is Satyavan. He's the one I've chosen in my heart. Notice who does the choosing here. It's the daughter, and it isn't a ceremony in a hall. She has gone out into the world and come back with a name. And sitting at the king's side, Narada has heard it. He's about to speak.
screen: `A FATHER'S LONG DISCIPLINE.` · `TOO RADIANT TO BE ASKED.` · `"GO AND CHOOSE FOR YOURSELF."` · then, large: `SHE COMES HOME WITH A NAME.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, and let the breath slow. Savitri went out and looked for herself. Bring to mind one choice in your life that was truly your own, large or small: a friend, a path, a place, a word you said. Breathe in, and let yourself remember choosing it. Breathe out, and let it be what it is, without grading it. If other choices come to mind, the ones made for you, let them pass for now. If you pray, you can bring that choice into your prayer. If not, simply rest in having chosen. The bell holds the time.
Savitri. A princess too radiant for suitors to approach, sent out by her father to choose, who comes home with the name of an exiled king's son.
Your line: make one choice fully your own. Today, make one small choice fully your own, and notice how it feels to stand behind it. Day seven hundred ninety-five.

howItsDone: The story of Savitri and Satyavan is told by the sage Markandeya to Yudhishthira in the Vana Parva of the Mahabharata, and Savitri is remembered in Hindu observance, including the Vat Savitri vrata kept by some married women.
